blocks.text: Model a small language as a class per grammar rule, so a sentence becomes a tree that evaluates itself.

Each rule of the grammar becomes a node type. **Terminal** nodes (numbers, variables) answer directly; **nonterminal** nodes (sums, comparisons) combine their children. Parsing builds the tree once, then `eval(context)` runs it as often as needed against different inputs.

items: **Fits:** small, stable grammars such as rules, filters, formulas and queries.
**Cost:** one class per rule; a large grammar becomes unmanageable.
**Separate concerns:** parsing builds the tree, the nodes only evaluate.

blocks.text: GoF Interpreter does not include the parser. For anything beyond a toy grammar, reach for a parser generator or an existing expression library.

walkthrough.note: The abstract expression. `sealed` closes the grammar: the compiler knows every node type, so adding a rule is a visible, deliberate change.
Terminal expressions end the recursion. `Var` reads from the context (the environment map), which is what makes one tree reusable across inputs.
Nonterminal expressions hold sub-expressions and delegate to them. Evaluation is a recursive walk with no central switch.
A tiny prefix parser builds the tree. It is separate from the nodes: the pattern defines the tree, not how you obtain it.
Parse once, evaluate with any environment. The printed record shows the abstract syntax tree the sentence became.

blocks.text: Operator-defined eligibility rules for a promotion.

Marketing wants to write conditions such as `plan = 'pro' and seats > 10` without a deploy. The rule text is parsed once at save time into an AST of `And`, `Equals` and `GreaterThan` nodes, validated, and cached. Each request evaluates the cached tree against a `Customer` context. The grammar has six rules and rarely grows, which is where Interpreter pays off.
Payoff: non-engineers change rules at runtime, and the same validated tree is evaluated on every request without reparsing.

lists.title: Use when
items: The grammar is small and stable, and sentences are evaluated repeatedly.
Users or config supply the rules, so they cannot be compiled in.
You want the tree itself to be inspectable, printable and testable.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The grammar is large or evolving: class count and maintenance explode.
Performance is critical; tree walking is slower than compiled code.
A lambda, `Predicate` or existing expression engine already does the job.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating hand-written string splitting as a parser and getting precedence wrong.
Evaluating untrusted input with unbounded recursion depth or cost.
Mixing parsing into the nodes, which couples syntax to semantics.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Sealed interfaces plus records give a closed, immutable AST.
A `switch` over the sealed type can host several operations outside the nodes, like Visitor.

rows.difference: An interpreter tree is a Composite whose leaves and branches carry grammar meaning. Composite is about treating parts and wholes uniformly; Interpreter adds evaluation of a language.
Visitor moves operations such as eval, print and optimize out of the nodes, so you can add them without editing every node class. Natural once the grammar is stable.
Terminal symbols that repeat (constants, keywords) can be shared as flyweights to save memory in big trees.
If you only need to pick one of a few algorithms, a strategy or lambda is enough. Interpreter is for sentences with structure that users compose.
An iterator can walk the tree for tooling such as pretty-printing or validation, without adding methods to each node.

modelAnswer.text: Interpreter turns each rule of a small grammar into a class. A parsed sentence is a tree of those nodes, and evaluating the root recursively evaluates the whole sentence against a context. Parsing is separate from the pattern. It suits small, stable grammars; for large ones use a parser generator or an existing engine.

keyPoints: One class per grammar rule: terminals and nonterminals
The sentence is an AST that evaluates itself against a context
Parsing builds the tree and is not part of the pattern
Does not scale to large or changing grammars
Structurally a Composite with language semantics
